h2. Description

Resolve ovnkube node encap IP from environment variable.

The ovnkube-node wrapper now derives the {{--encap-ip}} value from the {{OVN_ENCAP_IP}} environment variable. This enables per-node encap IP configuration, allowing each node to receive its own encapsulation IP when needed.

{{OVN_ENCAP_IP}} is expected to be set through the {{env-overrides}} ConfigMap. For example:

{code:yaml}apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: env-overrides
  namespace: openshift-ovn-kubernetes
data:
  ocp-virt-ctlplane-0.lab: |
    OVN_ENCAP_IP=10.0.0.1
  ocp-virt-worker-0.lab: |
    OVN_ENCAP_IP=10.0.0.2
  ocp-virt-worker-1.lab: |
    OVN_ENCAP_IP=10.0.0.3
  ocp-virt-worker-2.lab: |
    OVN_ENCAP_IP=10.0.0.4{code}

Expected behavior: when {{OVN_ENCAP_IP}} is set on a node, ovnkube-node uses that value for {{--encap-ip}}. If the variable is not set, existing behavior remains unchanged.

h3. Summary

Research whether the proposed OVN-K8s topology change is compatible with all features.

h3. Context

The parent Epic proposes changing the OVN-K8s topology to introduce a router in the path between UDN Gateway Routers and br-ex. This is intended to solve ARP/Broadcast issues.

One of the initial concerns is that BGP routes may need to be installed on the new router instead of on the UDN GR. This could cause issues if each UDN has different routes, such as when they are using VRF.

h3. Acceptance criteria

* Confirm whether it is compatible with all existing OVN-K8s and UDN features, including BGP.
* Confirm whether it is compatible with future planned changes to OVN-K8s for DPU offload.
* Confirm whether it supports removing double SNAT from Pod IP → Masquerade IP → Node IP.

items.toString: This work item links to "https://github.com/ovn-kubernetes/ovn-kubernetes/pull/6417/changes/459830498a7e7caf9fbd104c460a8c539ee68387 (Web Link)"

The KubeVirt live migration/restart keep-IP e2e fails for secondary localnet dual-stack UDNs after the Kubernetes/KubeVirt bump. The VM starts correctly and OVN/Multus allocate both IPv4 and IPv6, but KubeVirt VMI status reports only the IPv4 address for the secondary interface.

The test was treating VMI status as the source of truth for the full dual-stack allocation and expected two addresses. In failing CI runs, VMI status contained only one address, for example:

{{Expected ["10.4.48.8"] to have length 2 Expected ["10.36.176.6"] to have length 2}}

Logs showed the secondary interface allocation still existed in pod/Multus/network-status/virt-handler with both IPv4 and IPv6. So the failure was a test assertion issue, not evidence that OVN lost the persistent IPv6 allocation.

*Affected Test*

{{Kubevirt Virtual Machines with user defined networks and persistent ips configured should keep ip after restart of VirtualMachine with Secondary/Localnet ingress snat [Feature:VirtualMachineSupport]}}

*Root Cause*

Secondary KubeVirt interfaces use IPv4-only guest configuration in this path because DHCPv6 on secondary interfaces is not supported. As a result, KubeVirt VMI status may omit the guest-invisible secondary IPv6 address even though OVN and Multus allocated it correctly.

*Fix*

Update the e2e test so that:

* Primary UDNs continue validating addresses from KubeVirt VMI status.
* Secondary UDNs validate the full allocated address set from the running virt-launcher pod Multus {{network-status}}.
* VMI status is still used for guest-visible addresses.
* The test compares allocated addresses before and after restart/migration so real persistent IP loss still fails.

Commit:

{{459830498 test: validate secondary KubeVirt IPs from pod status}}

Cherry-picked from earlier fix:

{{a019fbdc0 test: validate secondary KubeVirt IPs from pod status}}

*Acceptance Criteria*

* The secondary/localnet dual-stack KubeVirt keep-IP e2e no longer fails only because VMI status reports IPv4.
* The test still fails if OVN/Multus actually loses either allocated IP.
* No product code is changed.
* {{test/e2e/kubevirt.go}} compiles successfully.
* CI KubeVirt live migration lanes pass for local and shared gateway dual-stack jobs.

The idea is to make sure the the developer documentation in the docs sub-directory is properly structured to be referenced by other files distributed throughout the project where developers and AI agents might be sourcing from.

For example, and root level ARCHITECTURE.md would:

* reference docs/design/architecture.md which in turn should reference other documents within  docs/design, docs/features and others.
* reference an entry point to docs/developer-guide from which other references would be made within that folder

As another example, it might be interesting to integrate the information in .go-controller/README.md ./REVIEWING.md to somewhere in docs/developer-guide.

Yet another example is to break out from docs/design and docs/features what we consider user facing information from what we consider developer information or implementation details. So we would end up with clearly separate user-guide and developer-guide.

So again, the purpose here is to reorganize the information that we already have just adding what it is needed so that AI agents can navigate it adequately. 
The purpose is not to complete or correct the information itself, for which we will have specific stories.

items.fromString:
The top-level AGENTS.md file represents the entry point for AI agents to operate in the ovn-kubernetes project and repository.

There is some things to take into account when contextifying:

* AGENTS.md files themselves should be as small as possible and contain instructions only relevant for agents. 
* For the most part, they should contain pointers to other information sources that are as valuable for humans as they are for agents, unless there is a specific benefit from duplicating the information. 
* Big chunks of monolithic context should be avoided and principals of progressive disclosure followed. See [https://www.aihero.dev/a-complete-guide-to-agents-md|https://www.aihero.dev/a-complete-guide-to-agents-md|smart-link] and [https://agents.md/|https://agents.md/|smart-link] 

So the idea for the top level AGENTS.md file is to contain higher level instructions for AI agents and contain pointers to, for example:

* other subdirectory AGENTS.md files for lower level package specific instructions for AI
* an architecture section, maybe containing agent specific hints but mostly pointing to top level ARCHITECTURE.md file for architecture and design information
* a reviews section, maybe containing agent specific hints but mostly pointing to a REVIEWS.md file for review guidance that is as valuable for humans as it is for agents
* a build section, maybe containing agent specific hints but mostly pointing to BUILD.md file for build guidance that is as valuable for humans as it is for agents
* a tests section, maybe containing agent specific hints but mostly pointing to TESTS.md file for test guidance that is as valuable for humans as it is for agents
* a PR section, maybe containing agent specific hints but mostly pointing to PULL_REQUESTS.md file for PR writing guidance that is as valuable for humans as it is for agents
* and so on …

So an AGENTS.md file is like a README.md file but tailored for agents. Structurally it can be more concise, direct, and terse than a README.md file because it is for a machine to read.

For reference, there already exists a REVIEWING.md file that could be pointed to, and a go-controller/README.md with build/tests instructions.

There might also be overlap with information contained in docs. In that case, the idea is to copy the information over out of docs and later on somehow come up with a process that can build docs sourcing the information from other parts of the project.
